1.5 Normal Cost Layers for Gains/Losses After 2022
Gains and losses realized after 2022, create new amortization layers adjusting the normal cost 
and have the same amortization period as the Legacy Liability until the remaining period for the 
Legacy Liability is less than 20 years. When the remaining amortization period of the Legacy 
Liability is less than 20 years, new layers will be amortized over a closed 20-year period. 
1.6 Legacy Liability Payment Schedule
The RSVS performed as of December 31, 2022 created a Legacy Liability amortization schedule 
which establishes the payments the City of Austin is to contribute in addition to the ADC each 
year to retire the unfunded actuarial accrued liability. The entire schedule of Legacy Liability 
payments can be found at www.coaers.org/RFP.
1.7 Investments
As of March 31, 2025, COAERS held investments with fair value totaling $3.5 billion. The 
Board has found it prudent to diversify both across and within the major asset classes to
construct a portfolio that delivers strong compound returns on a long-term, risk-adjusted 
basis. The Board recently adopted a new strategic asset allocation as shown below. Note 
however, that it is expected to take some time to ramp up the private market’s elements of 
the new strategic asset allocation.

12
Investments are made with care, skill, prudence, and diligence under the circumstances then 
prevailing that a prudent person acting in a like capacity and familiar with such matters would 
use in the conduct of an enterprise of a like character and with like aims. Funds of COAERS are 
invested solely in the interest of the membership and their beneficiaries, and for the exclusive 
purpose of providing benefits to such membership and their beneficiaries while defraying 
reasonable expenses of administering COAERS. 
The Board of Trustees has established an Investment Policy Statement and related guidelines for 
the administration of the investment program. Moreover, an Investment Committee has been 
chartered to assist the Board with research, recommendations, and monitoring of the investment 
portfolio. Investment consulting services are provided by the Meketa Investment Group and 
COAERS employs four professionals to oversee day-to-day implementation activities of the
investment portfolio. 
1.8 Experience Studies
COAERS believes that a periodic review of our actuarial assumptions is crucial to understanding 
and managing the cost of the benefits promised to members of COAERS. The use of outdated 
or inappropriate assumptions can result in understated costs which will lead to higher future
contribution rates; or overstated costs which place an unnecessary financial burden on the City 
of Austin and its employees. Accordingly, COAERS conducts experience studies every five years. 
During each experience study, each assumption is reviewed and compared to the actual 
experience of the plan with consideration of adding in a slight margin for adverse experience. 
Then the assumptions, as a whole, are reviewed for reasonableness and consistency. COAERS
recently reviewed its actuarial assumptions based on census data as of December 31, 2024. 
Certain key assumptions are listed below. A full discussion of the assumptions can be found in 
the Experience Study Report at www.coaers/RFP.

SECTION TWO – CORE SCOPE OF SERVICES 
Respondents will use Exhibit H to provide an annual fixed price for the core scope of services as 
described in this section for each year of the five-year term. All other services provided will be 
priced as agreed to by COAERS by an annual Engagement Letter at the time of the request 
during the contract. 
2.1 Personnel
All services provided for the scope of services described herein must be performed under the 
direct supervision of a Supervising Actuary who have been regularly engaged in the business of 
providing actuarial services for at least 10 years and must have the designation of either an 
Associate or Fellow of the Society of Actuaries and/or Member of the American Academy of 
Actuaries. The Supervising Actuary must approve all the work provided to COAERS. The 
Respondent will identify the Supervising Actuary in its response.
2.2 Annual Actuarial Valuation (Including a Risk Sharing Valuation Study)
a) Description of Work: 
1) Measurements using the following actuarial methods:
i) Entry Age Normal Cost method will be used to allocate the cost of accruing benefits 
as a level percentage of pay over the period from the member’s entry into the plan 
until termination or retirement;
ii) Five-year smoothing method asset method which recognizes 20% of the differences 
between expected and actual investment income in the current and each 
subsequent year, with offsetting unrecognized gains and losses immediately
recognized; and a
iii) A declining 30-year amortization period to determine the payments on new liability 
layers until reaching 20-years, thereafter, using closed 20-year layers. The aggregate 
funding period for the system is the weighted average of the amortization layers. 
The goal is to eliminate negative amortization as soon as possible, but negative

ADMINISTRATIVE MATTERS 
Type of Entity
The City of Austin Employees’ Retirement System (COAERS) is a single employer governmental 
defined benefit retirement system originally established in 1941 by City ordinance and governed 
since 1991 by Texas statute (Vernon’s Ann.Texas Civ.St. Art. 6243n). COAERS is qualified under 
Section 401(a) of the Internal Revenue Code. 
COAERS Board of Trustees
The COAERS Board of Trustees is vested with the statutory power and responsibility for the 
proper and effective general administration, management, and operation of the retirement 
system for the exclusive benefit of its present and future members and beneficiaries. The Board 
consists of 11 members comprised of City of Austin officials, employees, retirees, and citizens.
Participating Employers
Two employers participate in the Plan, the City of Austin Texas with over 17,000 active and 
deferred members and 7,100 retirees and the City of Austin Employees Retirement System 
staff with 38 active and deferred members and 13 retirees. 
Authority for Actuarial Services 
The COAERS Board of Trustees has statutory authority for the selection of an actuary. The 
statute states the Board of Trustees shall designate an actuary who shall be the technical 
advisor of the retirement board regarding the maintenance and operations of the fund but 
not an investment advisor or fiduciary with respect to any investments of the fund. The 
statute directs the actuary to perform valuations of the assets and liabilities of the fund.
Actuarial Determine Contribution Plan
COAERS is an actuarial determined contribution (ADC) rate plan in which, each year, the 
actuary determines the normal cost of the plan as a percentage of pay adjusting for the 
administrative expense and any liability layers established after December 31, 2022. The 
total normal cost of the plan isthen forecasted for the upcoming year. The forecasted normal 
cost is reduced by the employee contribution rate to yield the upcoming years’ employer 
contribution rate. The statutory requirements for the plan, including the determination of 
the ADC, can be found in the COAERS statutes at TX CIV ST Art 6243n.

COAERS prepares an Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR) each year by using internal

1.1 Funding Approach in General
COAERS is an actuarial determined contribution (ADC) rate plan in which, each year, the actuary 
determines the normal cost of the plan as a percentage of pay adjusting for the administrative 
expense and amortization of any gain/loss layers (“liability layers) established after December 
31, 2022. The total normal cost of the plan is then forecasted for the upcoming year. The 
forecasted normal cost is reduced by the employee contribution rate to yield the upcoming years’ 
employer contribution rate. An existing amortization schedule of fixed payments, called Legacy 
Liability payments, has also been created to retire the plan’s Unfunded Actuarial Accrued 
Liability. The plan sponsor is required by law to make the required Legacy Liability payments in 
addition to the employer’s contribution each year. 
COAERS’ strategic funding objective is to meet the long-term pension obligations promised to 
all members of the plan. To meet this objective, COAERS has put in place a set of policies and 
legislative requirements to:
1. Establish a fixed payment schedule to pay off the Unfunded Actuarial Accrued Liability 
(UAAL) over a fixed, closed 30-year period, known as the Legacy Liability.
2. Conduct annual actuarial valuations, which include a Risk Sharing Valuation Study
(RSVS), to determine the ADC rate for the upcoming year for the employers participating 
in the plan (See TX CIV ST Art. 6243n for a full description of the state statute detailing 
the Risk Sharing Valuation Study).
3. Monitor the employer’s contribution rate relative to the expected future trajectory of 
the rate, known as a corridor midpoint.
4. If the employer portion of the ADC exceeds the corridor maximum (5% of pay above the 
corridor midpoint), take action to increase employee contributions up to the 2%
maximum, and discuss future changes to the Plan if the ADC exceeds the employer and 
employee maximums.
5. Periodically conduct Actuarial Experience Studies to review and adopt the assumptions 
and methods used to determine the cost of the promised benefits. State law requires 
Experience Studies to perform no less than every five years. The last Experience Study 
was conducted as of December 31, 2024.
1.2 Actuarial Determined Contribution
COAERS is an actuarially determined contribution (ADC) rate plan. The ADC is comprised of the 
normal cost and the administrative expense assumption adjusted for the amortization of any 
liability layers expressed as a percentage of pay. COAERS uses the Entry Age Normal actuarial 
cost method to develop the normal cost for each benefit component – retirement, termination, 
disability, etc. The administrative expense assumption is currently .70% of pay. 
In determining the future contribution rate, the actuary also determines if any adjustments are 
needed for gains or losses by way of additional liability layers. Such layers have already been 
established for 2023 and 2024 and will continue to be calculated each subsequent year. Future

10
actuarial losses are converted to a percentage of payroll, amortized, and the layer added to the 
normal cost. Future actuarial gains are converted to a percentage of payroll, amortized, and the 
layer subtracted from the normal cost. Based upon the result, the actuary then projects the 
normal cost for the future upcoming calendar year, and the employee contribution rate is 
subtracted to yield the employer contribution rate for the upcoming year.
In addition, a model of future expected employer contribution rates has also been established to 
help COAERS determine a range of future acceptable employer contribution rates. An Initial Risk 
Sharing Valuation Study (RSVS) was performed as of December 31, 2022 establishing a 
contribution rate corridor. The corridor has a midpoint which is the expected future trajectory 
of the employer contribution rate. Additionally, a minimum and a maximum employer 
contribution rate were also set at 5% of pay above and 5% of pay below the midpoint. This 
corridor provides COAERS with a range of possible future employer contribution rates. The 
contribution corridor is used to trigger important subsequent events. First, if the ADC would 
cause the employer contribution rate to exceed the corridor’s maximum contribution rate, then 
the employee contribution rate will have to increase accordingly. The increase would be added 
to the 10% current employee contribution rate up to an additional 2% of payroll to cover the 
shortfall. Second, if ADC exceeds the additional 2% of pay from the employees, then COAERS 
and the City of Austin must enter into discussions to come up with a plan to address the funding 
and the expense of the Plan. Finally, if the ADC is lower than the corridor midpoint, the employer 
contribution will remain at the corridor midpoint so long as the funded ratio is below 90%.

As of March 31, 2025, COAERS held investments with fair value totaling $3.5 billion. The 
Board has found it prudent to diversify both across and within the major asset classes to
construct a portfolio that delivers strong compound returns on a long-term, risk-adjusted 
basis. The Board recently adopted a new strategic asset allocation as shown below. Note 
however, that it is expected to take some time to ramp up the private market’s elements of 
the new strategic asset allocation.

Investments are made with care, skill, prudence, and diligence under the circumstances then 
prevailing that a prudent person acting in a like capacity and familiar with such matters would 
use in the conduct of an enterprise of a like character and with like aims. Funds of COAERS are 
invested solely in the interest of the membership and their beneficiaries, and for the exclusive 
purpose of providing benefits to such membership and their beneficiaries while defraying 
reasonable expenses of administering COAERS.

investment portfolio. 
1.8 Experience Studies
COAERS believes that a periodic review of our actuarial assumptions is crucial to understanding 
and managing the cost of the benefits promised to members of COAERS. The use of outdated 
or inappropriate assumptions can result in understated costs which will lead to higher future
contribution rates; or overstated costs which place an unnecessary financial burden on the City 
of Austin and its employees. Accordingly, COAERS conducts experience studies every five years. 
During each experience study, each assumption is reviewed and compared to the actual 
experience of the plan with consideration of adding in a slight margin for adverse experience. 
Then the assumptions, as a whole, are reviewed for reasonableness and consistency. COAERS
recently reviewed its actuarial assumptions based on census data as of December 31, 2024.

the Experience Study Report at www.coaers/RFP.

CITY OF GRAND RAPIDS POLICE AND FIRE RETIREMENT SYSTEM 
INVESTMENT CONSULTANT SERVICES 
REQUEST FOR PROPOSAL (“RFP”) 
RE: INVESTMENT CONSULTING SERVICES 
The City of Grand General Retirement System and the City of Grand Rapids Police and Fire 
Retirement System (collectively the “Plan”) are requesting proposals for Investment Consulting 
Services by 4:00 P.M. on Thursday, August 31, 2023. 
I. OVERVIEW
The Boards of Trustees of the City of Grand Rapids General Retirement System and City 
of Grand Rapids Police and Fire Retirement System (collectively the “Board”) are in the 
process of reviewing their investment consultant services. The purpose of this RFP is to 
gain adequate information from which the Boards may evaluate such services. This RFP 
includes detail on general (non-discretionary) and discretionary (OCIO) services. Firms are 
asked to submit proposals for either, or both, as appropriate. 
Further information about the Plan is available at https://grpensions.org/. 
City of Grand Rapids General Retirement System 
 The City of Grand Rapids General Retirement System has a total market value of 
approximately $437 Million as of June 30, 2023. 
 The Plan’s portfolio consists of approximately: 24% fixed income; 17% U.S. equity; 10% 
global equity; 8% non-U.S. equity; 8% ADRs; 8% private equity; 5% treasury inflation-protected securities; 5% real estate (REITs); 5% commodities; 5% mid-stream energy; and 
5% private credit. 
City of Grand Rapids Police and Fire Retirement System 
 The City of Grand Rapids Police and Fire Retirement System has a total market value of 
approximately $479 Million as of June 30, 2023. 
 The Plan’s portfolio consists of approximately: 23% fixed income; 19% U.S. equity; 10% 
global equity; 8% non-U.S. equity; 9% ADRs; 7% private equity; 5% treasury inflation-protected securities; 5% real estate (REITs); 5% commodities; 5% mid-stream energy; and 
4% private credit. 
Northern Trust currently serves as custodian for the Plan’s assets.

2 
A. SCOPE OF SERVICES
The primary role of the Investment Consultant is to provide objective, third-party 
advice and counsel that will enable the Board to make well-informed and well-educated decisions regarding the investment of Plan assets. 
 Contractual services for investment consulting will include, but not be limited to, 
the following: 
 1. Development Investment Policy, Objectives and Guidelines
 Assist the Board in the development and periodic review of a policy 
statement that properly reflects the Board’s tolerance for risk and that best 
helps the Board meet its rate-of-return, funded status and administrative 
expense objectives. 
 
 2. Asset Allocation Studies
 Conduct periodic asset allocation studies to determine whether or not the 
current asset allocation falls within the Board's investment objectives and 
guidelines. 
 3. Investment Manager Search 
 When deemed necessary, assist the Board in its due diligence and search for 
new investment manager(s) utilizing the appropriate data base. 
 4. Development of Investment Manager Performance 
 Standards/Guidelines
Assist the Board in the development and review of performance standards 
and guidelines with which the Board can measure each investment
manager's progress. Attend monthly meetings or special meetings as 
requested by the Board. 
 5. General Consulting Services
 Provide general consulting services as requested by the Board. These might 
include custodial search and selection, etc. 
 6. Performance Measurement & Monitoring
 Monitor the performance of the investment manager(s) to provide the Board 
with the ability to determine the manager’s progress toward achieving the 
Board’s investment objectives. Prepare and provide written quarterly 
reports submitted to the Board.

3 
 7. Monitor compliance with Act 314
 Monitor the investment of the Plan’s assets consistent with the limitations 
under Public Act 314 of 1965, as amended, with written quarterly reports 
submitted to the Board. 
8. Assist in Fund Diversification/Asset Management
 Assist the Board in the development of an investment manager structure 
that provides adequate diversification with respect to the number and types 
of investment managers to be retained by the Board. 
9. Historical Information Related to Specific Holdings 
 
 Upon request, provide information regarding the holdings, sale and 
purchase of specific equities in order to complete proof of claims related to 
securities litigation. 
10. Discretionary Investment Management Services (OPTIONAL)
 Fully discretionary investment management services, should the boards opt 
to enter into an OCIO agreement. 
B. MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS
1. The Investment Consultant must have a minimum of five (5) years of 
experience in providing institutional investor consulting services. 
2. The Investment Consultant must provide services to at least one (1) public 
employee retirement system with at least $250 million in assets. 
3. The Investment Consultant must be a registered investment advisor under 
the Investment Advisors Act of 1940. 
4. The Investment Consultant shall acknowledge its responsibilities as an 
investment fiduciary under Public Act 314 of 1965, as amended. 
5. If you are affiliating or partnering with a national firm, or are a local office 
of a national firm, the minimum qualification requirements herein must be 
satisfied by the individual or entity submitting this proposal.
6. The Investment Consultant must attend regular meetings, as well as special 
meetings upon request by the Board, at no additional cost to the Plan. 
 The Board currently meets nine times per year.

4

 To achieve a uniform review process and obtain the maximum degree of 
comparability, it is required that the submission be organized in the following 
manner: 
 1. Title Page: 
 Please indicate the RFP subject, the name of your organization, address, 
telephone number, name of contact person and date. 
 2. Table of Contents: 
 Clearly identify the material by section and page number. 
 3. Response to Request for Proposal: 
Please respond to each question in order of sequence in the Request for 
Proposal (Section II). 
 4. Submission: 
 The Board requests that one (1) copy of your response be submitted to the 
Plan in a sealed envelope clearly marked as follows: 
 
 RFP: Investment Consulting Services 
 City of Grand Rapids Retirement Systems 
 233 East Fulton, Suite 216 
 Grand Rapids, Michigan 49503 
The Board also requests that an electronic copy of your response be 
provided via email to: 
Peggy Korzen, Executive Director: info@grpensions.org
Thomas Michaud, Legal Counsel: tmichaud@vmtlaw.com

seven (7) days prior to the due date for proposals and shall be directed to 
Peggy Korzen, at the email address provided above. All questions received 
after the deadline established herein shall not be considered. 
Please indicate your intent to respond, via email to info@grpensions.org, no 
later than 4:00 p.m. on Tuesday, August 15, 2023. 
 Your response to this RFP must be received at the above address by 4:00 
p.m. on August 31, 2023. Late RFP responses will not be considered or 
accepted.

5 
 
II. REQUEST FOR PROPOSAL – Please label each response with the corresponding 
question’s section and number.
A. FIRM INFORMATION
1. Name of your firm, its address, telephone number, and primary contact for 
the request for proposal. Give the names of the persons who will be 
authorized to make presentations for your organization, their titles, 
addresses, and telephone numbers. 
2. Briefly state your organization’s understanding of the nature of the work. 
3. Is your organization a subsidiary, parent, or affiliate of any other firm? If 
so, please describe in detail. Also, do any of these affiliates provide any 
other retirement plan services such as investment management, actuarial 
work, custodial, etc.? If you provide more than one service, how do you 
protect against conflicts of interest? Have you ever included your own firm, 
subsidiary or sponsored investment vehicle in a manager search you are 
conducting? 
4. What is the number of full-time employees in your firm? How many 
professionals have separated employment from your company in the last 3 
years? 
5. What is the location of your nearest office to the City of Grand Rapids? 
6. Please submit biographical profiles on the individual(s) who will be 
assigned to our account. Also, where are these individuals located? Who 
will attend meetings? Be specific as to the individual’s consulting 
experience. 
7. What public funds experience does your firm have? Provide a list of all 
public pension fund clients under contract to date. Please provide a 
minimum of 3 references by name of client, type of client, contact person, 
address and telephone number. Please populate the table below as of 
6/30/2023. If a different date is used, please note the as of date. 
National Michigan
# Plans $1,000,000,000 and greater
# Plans $250,000,000 to $999,999,999
# Plans $100,000,000 to $249,999,999
# Plans $0 to$99,999,999
Total Public Fund AUA 
8. Has your firm has lost any clients in the last 3 years? If so, please explain 
and indicate whether the client was discretionary or non-discretionary.

6 
9. Please explain size, composition, and source of your performance 
measurement data base. What indices are used for relative comparisons? If 
you do not maintain databases, whose database do you use? 
10. Why is your firm uniquely qualified to service our account(s)? 
11. Disclose all formal or informal business relationships with investment 
managers or other service providers to trust funds. 
12. Provide as an attachment to your response a complete copy of your most 
recent form ADV as filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. 
13. What is your firm’s position on commission recapture programs and how 
would the Plans’ participation in such programs impact your services? 
14. Is your firm a member of the Michigan Association of Public Employee 
Retirement Systems (MAPERS)? 
15. Would your firm provide an on-site due diligence visit as a part of the 
evaluation process? If yes, please detail and provide a sample agenda. 
B. INVESTMENT POLICY/ASSET ALLOCATION GUIDELINES
1. Provide an outline of the steps you would follow when developing a 
statement of Investment Policy and Objectives. Does your investment 
policy and asset allocation analysis fully integrate liabilities with assets? 
How do you interface with the Plan’s actuary? 
2. How many meetings would be required with the Board throughout this 
process? Who would attend from your firm? 
3. Provide an outline of the issues and items that would be covered in a typical 
investment policy statement. 
4. What is your approach to development of asset allocation guidelines? 
Please describe this process in detail, including application of major 
variables (e.g. - risk tolerance, emerging liabilities, etc.). 
5. What asset classes are included in your work? 
6. What geographic areas of the world do you consider appropriate for Plan 
asset investments? 
7. Does your approach include passive strategies such as indexing? If so, 
please describe.

7 
 C. INVESTMENT MANAGER SELECTION
1. What is the procedure and criteria you follow in the selection of investment 
managers? What is the typical timeframe from start to finish? 
2. How many firms do you track for manager search purposes? 
3. Do the individual consultants assigned to our account interface with 
prospective managers? If so, please explain your due diligence process. 
4. What resources do you utilize for manager screening? Which are purchased 
and which are proprietary? 
5. Explain how you monitor and measure the level of success of existing 
managers. Please be specific. 
6. What criteria is used to recommend termination of a manager?
7. Do you believe that when a manager is not performing that the consultant 
who presented this manager also be held accountable? If so, how? If not, 
why? 
8. Do you have any arrangements with broker-dealers under which you or a 
related company will benefit if money managers place trades for their 
clients with such broker-dealers? 
 D. PERFORMANCE EVALUATION
1. Specifically describe your performance evaluation system and the 
philosophy behind it. Is your system propriety or did you obtain it from 
another supplier? 
2. How soon following the end of a reporting period can you have copies of 
evaluation reports to the Plan? How frequently do you recommend 
performance evaluation reviews? 
3. Provide samples of your standard reports. How much variation is available 
from your standard report? 
4. Describe and illustrate any special indices constructed by your firm. 
5. Please describe, in detail, the optimal role that your firm would like to take 
with the Plan. What other services are provided to your clients? 
6. Please provide 1, 3, 5 and 10 year performance results on an annualized 
(calendar year) basis for 3 of your non-discretionary public employee plan 
clients. If possible, these clients should include all Michigan public 
employee plans. The performance results should be based upon the period

8 
in which you served as the investment consultant and include, at a 
minimum, total fund performance on an annualized basis as of December 
31, 2022 with a comparison against the appropriate policy index. Said 
performance results may also include a breakdown of fund performance by 
asset class with the appropriate benchmark index and peer group rankings. 
Please identify each client by the size of its total plan assets, its asset 
allocation and the state in which it is located. You may also provide any 
appropriate commentary explaining over/under performance and your role 
in the investment process. 
7. Does your firm complete “proof of claim” documents on behalf of clients 
in securities actions? Is there a fee for this service? 
8. How would you recommend the Board evaluate its investment consultant? 
9. How does your firm monitor brokerage services? (i.e., best cost and 
execution) 
 E. CUSTODIAL SERVICES
1. Does your firm provide custodial services? If so, please provide 
details. 
F. DISCRETIONARY INVESTMENT MANAGEMENT SERVICES
1. Do you provide discretionary investment management services (i.e., 
OCIO)? If yes, please answer the following questions. 
2. How long has your firm offered discretionary services? What portion of 
your firm’s revenue comes from discretionary/OCIO? 
3. Indicate the total pension assets currently under discretionary management 
by your firm, and the total pension assets currently under non-discretionary 
advisement by your firm. 
4. Describe your firm’s investment philosophy and strategy including, but not 
limited to, research efforts, account construction guidelines, risk control 
techniques and rebalancing strategy. 
5. Describe how you would factor the Plan’s investment goals and risk 
preferences into your firm’s approach. 
6. Explain your firm’s view on passive versus active management. What is 
your firm’s recommended allocation, if any, between active and passive 
management? 
7. Briefly summarize your philosophy regarding the overall level of cash you 
typically maintain in a pension portfolio.

9 
8. Please provide an overview of your current portfolio positioning, and 
indicate how long you have held those views. Do your OCIO clients follow 
a model portfolio, or are portfolios custom to each client? 
9. Describe your firm’s experience with alternative asset classes, including 
private equity, private credit, and similar alternative investments. 
10. Describe the role you expect alternative asset classes to play in the portfolio. 
11. What trade-offs do you typically see between public and private market 
allocations? Please make sure that your answer reflects the current market 
environment and investment landscape.

process? Describe your connectivity with the Plan’s actuary. 
13. Describe your customary range of target allocations for equities, fixed 
income and alternative assets currently being recommended to clients with 
underfunded / overfunded pension plans. 
14. Briefly identify the three attributes of your firm’s manager research 
philosophy and process that lead you to identify superior performing 
managers. This is intended to go beyond the traditional description of 
people, philosophy, process and performance and into the resources, tools 
and approach that allow you to select managers that can create alpha. 
15. When transitioning a plan’s assets for a new client/account, does your firm 
liquidate current holdings and transition in cash? How do you handle 
existing illiquid investments such as private equity and private real estate? 
16. Please describe your policies and procedures concerning trading and 
execution, including those relating to (i) how your firm seeks to achieve 
best execution; (ii) how your firm ensures equitable trading for all clients 
(i.e., the account of one client is not favored above the account of another) 
and exceptions to this policy, if any; (iii) allocation of trades (e.g., by 
portfolio manager or automated). 
17. What do you see as the pros and cons of a discretionary investment manager 
versus a non-discretionary investment fiduciary? 
18. Who is your current fiduciary bond carrier? 
19. Provide a copy of your disaster recovery plan. 
20. Provide a copy of your business conduct/ethics policy. 
21. Indicate the policies and procedures your firm has established to ensure

10 
compliance with your clients’ investment policy statements and guidelines 
you may have adopted to ensure quality control over the asset management 
process. 
 G. FEES
1. Please indicate in detail your fee schedule (e.g., investment performance 
analysis services, asset allocation, investment policy, manager search, 
custodial search, custodial services, etc.). 
 If your firm provides discretionary investment management services, please 
provide specific cost details. 
 If your fee is based on a percentage of Plan assets, please also quote your 
service on a hard dollar basis. 
2. Would you charge separately for travel expenses? If so, explain in detail 
your policy. 
 3. What other costs or expenses might we incur with your firm? 
 4. Do you offer payment on a pro rata quarterly basis billed in arrears? 
5. If services are also quoted on a soft dollar basis, what is the cost in cents per 
share? What is the commission to cash conversion ratio? Also, how do you 
report to a client on soft dollars received? 
6. What percentage of typical equity managers trades do you feel should be 
used for client directed brokerage purposes? 
7. Please provide all complaints received by the Securities and Exchange 
Commission (SEC) and the National Association of Securities Dealers. 
8. Has your firm been involved in litigation within the last five years or is there 
any pending litigation arising out of your performance? If your answer is 
yes, explain fully. 
9. Has your firm been investigated by any state or federal regulatory or law 
enforcement agency in the last ten years? If yes, please describe in detail 
the substance and results of each such investigation. 
10. Has your organization been a party to any lawsuit, including suits involving 
misfeasance or professional negligence, within the last ten years? If so, 
please describe the substance and results of each suit. 
11. Are you registered with the SEC or a state securities regulator as an 
investment adviser? If so, have you provided all the disclosures required 
under those laws?

11 
12. Do you or a related company have relationships with money managers that 
you recommend, consider for recommendation, or otherwise mention to the 
plan for our consideration? If so, describe those relationships? 
13. Do you or a related company receive any payments from money managers 
you recommend, consider for recommendation, or otherwise mention to the 
plan for our consideration? If so, what is the extent of these payments in 
relation to your other income (revenue)? 
14. Do you have any policies or procedures to address conflicts of interest or to 
prevent these payments or relationships from being considered when you 
provide advice to your clients? 
15. If you allow plans to pay your consulting fees using a plan's brokerage 
commissions, how do you monitor the commissions paid and report to the 
plan? 
16. If you allow plans to pay your consulting fees using the plan's brokerage 
commissions, what steps do you take to ensure that the plan receives best 
execution for its securities trades? 
17. Do you have any arrangements with broker-dealers under which you or a 
related company will benefit if money managers place trades for their 
clients with such broker-dealers? 
18. Will you acknowledge in writing that you have a fiduciary obligation as an 
investment adviser to the plan while providing the consulting services we 
are seeking? 
19. Do you consider yourself a fiduciary with respect to the recommendations 
you provide the plan? 
20. What percentage of your institutional clients utilize money managers, 
investment funds, brokerage services or other service providers from whom 
you receive fees? 
21. Describe the various types of insurance and indemnification provided to 
protect clients of service(s) proposed, including specific dollar coverage. 
 OTHER REQUIREMENTS
1. Pre-Qualification: Inviting a response does not assume a "pre-qualification" 
of any proposer. 
2. Preparation Cost: The Board will not be liable for any costs incurred in 
preparation of submissions.

12 
3. Certification as to "Request for Proposal" Content: By submitting a 
proposal, it is understood and agreed that the responder has fully read and 
understands the "Request for Proposal" and has full knowledge of the scope, 
nature, quantity, and quality of work to be performed. Unless specified to 
the contrary, submitting a proposal will be interpreted as agreement to all 
provisions in and requirements of the RFP. 
4. Additional Information and Instruction: The responder shall furnish such 
additional information as the Board may reasonably require. The Board 
reserves the right to investigate the qualifications of all responders as it 
deems appropriate. 
5. Consultants are requested NOT to contact individual trustees during this 
RFP process. Any attempt by a proposer to initiate contact with any 
member of the Plan, other than the designated contacts, may disqualify the 
proposer from further consideration. 
6. Rejection: The Board reserves the right to reject any or all proposals, the 
right in its sole discretion to accept the proposal which it considers most 
favorable to the Board's interest, and the right to waive minor irregularities 
in the procedures. The Board further reserves the right to seek new 
proposals when such a procedure is in its best interest. 
7. Binding for 90 Days: All proposals submitted shall be binding for ninety 
(90) calendar days following the above due date for receipt of proposals to 
allow for evaluation. 
8. Timeliness: Proposals received by the Board after the time specified for 
opening will not be considered. 
9. Completeness: All information required by the Request for Proposal shall 
be supplied to constitute an acceptable submission. 
The Plan appreciates the time and effort you will have expended in responding to this RFP. Thank 
you.

# Markdown Briefing

## IMRF Sample RFP: Required Meeting Attendance

Under **Section 3.1(G)** of the IMRF sample RFP, the investment consultant must attend the following meetings with **IMRF Board Members and/or Staff**, both **on-site and off-site**:

- **Monthly IMRF Board meetings**
- **Investment Committee meetings**
- **Annual IMRF Roundtable**
- **Regional meetings with investment managers**
- **Related investment meetings and discussions**
- **Formal interviews with existing and potential investment managers**
- **Ad hoc due diligence meetings with investment managers and Staff**

## Additional Attendance Detail

The RFP further specifies that a **Principal** is to:

- Attend the **monthly Investment Committee** meetings
- Attend the **monthly Board of Trustees** meetings
- Attend and assist with the **annual Regional Manager meetings**
- Attend and assist with the **annual Roundtable meeting**

## IMRF’s Estimated Annual Meeting Time

IMRF estimates that these responsibilities will require **sixty days of meetings per year** with the **Board of Trustees and/or Staff**.
